definition: On-demand network access to a shared pool of computing resources that can be provisioned and released quickly.
wrongs: A private mainframe that only local terminals on one campus can reach.
Buying and racking servers that stay dedicated to one application forever.
A peer-to-peer file share with no provider-managed resource pool.
why: NIST describes a shared, elastic pool that users provision over the network with little manual setup.
example: A lab starts virtual servers from a browser for a weekend project and deletes them on Monday.
scenario: A course project needs servers for three days, created from a portal and billed only for that use. Which delivery model fits?
scenarioWhy: Short-lived, self-served, pooled resources delivered over the network are cloud computing.

definition: A cloud service that supplies virtual machines, storage, and networks while the customer manages the operating system and applications.
wrongs: A finished application, such as webmail, run entirely by the provider.
A managed application runtime where the customer deploys only code.
A physical server shipped to the customer's own machine room.
why: The provider virtualises hardware; the customer still patches the guest OS and runs the software stack.
example: A team rents Linux virtual machines, chooses the kernel packages, and installs its own database.
scenario: A customer receives virtual machines and disks but must patch the guest operating system. Which service model is that?
scenarioWhy: Virtual infrastructure with customer-managed operating systems is IaaS.

definition: A cloud service that provides a managed runtime so the customer deploys application code without operating the servers.
wrongs: Raw virtual machines where the customer installs and patches the OS.
A complete end-user application such as hosted email.
Only object storage with no place to run code.
why: The provider runs the platform, language runtime, and scaling hooks; the customer supplies the app.
example: A student uploads a web app and the platform builds, runs, and restarts it without a chosen VM image.
scenario: Developers deploy application code onto a managed runtime and never log in to patch a server. Which service model is that?
scenarioWhy: A provider-managed runtime for customer code is PaaS.

definition: A finished application delivered over the network and operated entirely by the provider.
wrongs: Virtual machines on which the customer installs any software.
A runtime where the customer still ships and versions the application code.
A backup tape stored in the customer's office.
why: Users consume the application; the provider manages code, platform, and infrastructure.
example: Staff use a browser-based payroll system and never install or patch that application.
scenario: Employees open hosted email in a browser, and the vendor runs the whole application. Which service model is that?
scenarioWhy: A complete provider-operated application is SaaS.

definition: Cloud infrastructure offered to many unrelated customers by a third-party provider over the internet.
wrongs: Infrastructure operated solely for one organisation.
A cloud shared only by members of one industry consortium.
An air-gapped cluster with no external tenants.
why: Any customer who can pay may use the same provider services, isolated logically from other tenants.
example: A startup creates an account at a hyperscale provider and launches servers beside unknown other customers.
scenario: Anyone with a credit card can rent compute from the same provider on shared infrastructure. Which deployment model is that?
scenarioWhy: A provider service open to the general public is a public cloud.

definition: Cloud infrastructure operated for the exclusive use of a single organisation.
wrongs: A pool sold to any customer on the public internet.
A cloud shared by several universities under one consortium.
A single laptop running one local virtual machine for a class.
why: The organisation is the only tenant, whether the equipment sits on premises or at a host.
example: A bank runs a self-service virtual-machine portal that only its own business units can use.
scenario: Only one company's departments can provision resources on an elastic internal portal. Which deployment model is that?
scenarioWhy: Exclusive use by one organisation is a private cloud.

definition: A combination of private and public clouds linked so workloads and data can move between them.
wrongs: Two public regions of the same provider with no private site.
A private cloud that never connects to an outside provider.
A community cloud used by one research group only.
why: The defining feature is portability across distinct cloud deployments, often private plus public.
example: A hospital keeps records on its private cloud and bursts analytics jobs to a public region.
scenario: Sensitive systems stay in the company data centre while overflow web traffic runs at a public provider, connected by a private link. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Joined private and public deployments form a hybrid cloud.

definition: Cloud infrastructure shared by several organisations that have a common mission or compliance need.
wrongs: A cloud open to any paying customer worldwide.
Infrastructure dedicated to only one company.
A temporary lab account on a student's laptop.
why: The tenants share concerns such as a regulation or research mission, and share the cloud's cost and governance.
example: Several public universities share one research cloud built for the same data-protection rules.
scenario: Four hospitals jointly fund a cloud that only they may use, because they share the same health-data rules. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: A cloud limited to a group with a shared concern is a community cloud.

definition: A software-defined computer that runs its own operating system on virtual hardware.
wrongs: A process package that shares the host kernel and does not boot its own OS.
A physical blade server welded into one rack position.
An object stored under a key in a bucket.
why: A hypervisor presents virtual CPU, memory, and disks so a guest OS runs as if it had a machine.
example: One physical host runs a Windows guest and a Linux guest, each with its own virtual disk.
scenario: An administrator boots a full guest operating system on virtual CPU and disk allocated by a hypervisor. Which construct is that?
scenarioWhy: A guest operating system on virtual hardware is a virtual machine.

definition: Software that creates and runs virtual machines and divides the host's hardware among them.
wrongs: A load balancer that only forwards HTTP requests.
A container engine that shares one kernel among processes.
A billing report of hours consumed last month.
why: It schedules guest CPU and memory and traps privileged instructions so guests stay isolated.
example: A type-1 hypervisor on a server hosts twenty guest machines and pauses one to free RAM.
scenario: A layer under several guest operating systems allocates CPU and memory and keeps the guests apart. Which component is that?
scenarioWhy: The component that runs guest machines on shared hardware is the hypervisor.

definition: A lightweight isolated package that runs an application while sharing the host operating-system kernel.
wrongs: A virtual machine that boots a separate guest kernel.
A block volume attached as a raw disk.
A public IP address assigned to a subnet.
why: Isolation uses kernel features such as namespaces, so there is no second operating system to boot.
example: A web process and its libraries start in seconds on a worker that already runs the host Linux kernel.
scenario: An application starts in under a second, isolated from neighbours, but uses the worker's existing kernel. Which package is that?
scenarioWhy: Process isolation on a shared kernel is a container.

definition: Automated placement, scaling, and restart of containers across a cluster of machines.
wrongs: Manually copying one container onto a single laptop.
Partitioning a disk into volumes.
Negotiating a yearly discount with a vendor.
why: A control plane schedules containers, replaces failed copies, and rolls out new versions.
example: After a worker node dies, the cluster starts replacement web containers on remaining nodes.
scenario: A control plane notices a dead node and starts new copies of the web containers elsewhere. Which capability is that?
scenarioWhy: Automatically placing and healing containers on a cluster is orchestration.

definition: The ability to grow or shrink allocated resources automatically as demand changes.
wrongs: A fixed server size chosen once and never changed.
Moving an office printer closer to users.
Encrypting disks so they can be copied off site.
why: Cloud resources are meant to match the current load and be released when the load falls.
example: A ticket site adds application instances during a sale and removes them when the queue disappears.
scenario: Instances appear during a traffic spike and disappear after midnight when traffic returns to normal. Which property is that?
scenarioWhy: Resources that track demand up and down show elasticity.

definition: Increasing capacity by adding more machines or instances that share the work.
wrongs: Adding CPU and memory to the same single instance.
Compressing responses so one server sends fewer bytes.
Moving the database to a larger disk letter.
why: Scale-out adds workers beside the existing ones instead of enlarging one machine.
example: A web tier grows from four virtual machines to twelve during registration week.
scenario: To handle more logins, operators add six more identical web servers behind the load balancer. Which scaling direction is that?
scenarioWhy: Adding more instances to share load is horizontal scaling.

definition: Increasing capacity by giving an existing instance more CPU, memory, or storage.
wrongs: Adding more separate instances behind a load balancer.
Caching content on distant edge servers.
Splitting a monolith into network calls only.
why: Scale-up enlarges one machine rather than adding peers.
example: A database virtual machine is resized from 4 vCPUs to 16 vCPUs during exam week.
scenario: A single database instance is resized from 16 GB of RAM to 64 GB, with no extra replicas. Which scaling direction is that?
scenarioWhy: Enlarging one instance is vertical scaling.

definition: A named geographic area in which a provider operates one or more groups of data centres.
wrongs: A single rack inside an availability zone.
A virtual private subnet with one CIDR block.
The set of users allowed to call an API.
why: Regions let customers place workloads near users and choose a legal location for data.
example: A European shop launches its servers in a Paris region so pages load quickly for local buyers.
scenario: An architect picks a provider area in Singapore, containing several isolated data-centre groups, to host an app. Which area is that?
scenarioWhy: A geographic provider area of data centres is a region.

definition: An isolated data-centre group inside a region, with separate power and networking from its neighbours.
wrongs: A whole continent served by one provider brand.
A logical folder for objects in a bucket.
A single process inside a container.
why: Failure of one zone's power or network should not take down the other zones in that region.
example: A database keeps a synchronous replica in a second zone of the same region.
scenario: A fire in one data-centre group leaves the other groups in the same region running. Which isolated group failed?
scenarioWhy: An isolated data-centre group inside a region is an availability zone.

definition: Storage of unstructured blobs addressed by a key, usually through an HTTP API rather than a mounted disk.
wrongs: A raw volume that a virtual machine formats as a file system.
CPU registers inside a guest.
A message topic that deletes each event after delivery.
why: Each object has a key and metadata, and the service scales without presenting a traditional block device.
example: A photo app stores each image under a key such as albums/2026/img-18.jpg and fetches it with HTTPS.
scenario: An app uploads a video with a key and later downloads that blob over HTTPS, without formatting a disk. Which storage type is that?
scenarioWhy: Key-addressed blobs over HTTP are object storage.

definition: Storage presented to a virtual machine as a raw disk volume that the guest can format.
wrongs: Key-addressed blobs fetched with HTTP.
A content cache at a city edge node.
An in-memory session on a load balancer.
why: The guest sees sectors, like a hard disk, and usually builds its own file system on the volume.
example: A database VM formats an attached 500 GB volume with a file system and stores its data files there.
scenario: A virtual machine is given a raw 200 GB disk, which the guest formats before use. Which storage type is that?
scenarioWhy: A volume that behaves like a disk is block storage.

definition: Distributing incoming requests across several healthy servers so no single server takes all the work.
wrongs: Storing objects under keys in one bucket.
Encrypting traffic between two specific hosts only.
Reserving a discount for a one-year virtual machine.
why: A balancer spreads load and can skip servers that fail their health checks.
example: An HTTPS front end sends each new student login to one of eight application servers.
scenario: Incoming requests are spread across eight web servers, and a failed server receives none. Which function does the front end perform?
scenarioWhy: Spreading requests across healthy servers is load balancing.

definition: During a network partition, a distributed store must trade off consistency against availability.
wrongs: A rule that every cloud bill is capped at a fixed monthly price.
A proof that caches are always faster than disks.
A claim that encryption removes the need for access control.
why: If nodes cannot talk, they cannot both stay perfectly in sync and answer every request.
example: When a link between two database sites fails, designers either reject writes or accept temporary disagreement.
scenario: A partition splits a database. Designers either refuse some requests or allow replicas to disagree for a while. Which theorem frames that choice?
scenarioWhy: Choosing consistency or availability during a partition is the CAP tradeoff.

definition: A guarantee that replicas may disagree briefly but will converge if updates stop.
wrongs: Every read sees the latest write at every replica immediately.
Data are deleted on purpose after a retention timer.
A backup that is never restored or compared.
why: The system favours availability and reconciles copies after communication resumes.
example: A profile photo updated in one region appears in another region a few seconds later.
scenario: Two replicas of a shopping cart differ for a second after a write, then match once updates pause. Which consistency model is that?
scenarioWhy: Temporary disagreement that later converges is eventual consistency.

definition: Running short-lived functions on demand without the customer provisioning or managing servers.
wrongs: Renting a virtual machine that stays up and is patched by the customer.
Colocating a physical server the customer owns.
Editing infrastructure only by clicking, with no code.
why: The platform starts a function for an event, scales it, and bills for the execution used.
example: Uploading a file triggers a function that makes a thumbnail, and no server is left running afterward.
scenario: Image uploads invoke a function, the platform scales it, and the team never patches a host. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Event-driven functions without customer-managed servers are serverless computing.

definition: Extra latency when a serverless platform must create a new execution environment before running a function.
wrongs: The time to fail over a database to another availability zone.
The delay of a CDN cache hit served from memory.
The boot time of a physical machine delivered by courier.
why: After idle time the platform may have no warm environment, so it must initialise runtime and code.
example: The first request to an idle function takes 800 ms, while the next request on the warm copy takes 20 ms.
scenario: After an hour with no traffic, the next function call is much slower because a new environment must be built. Which delay is that?
scenarioWhy: Initialising a fresh serverless environment causes a cold start.

definition: The split in which the provider secures the cloud platform and the customer secures data, access, and configuration.
wrongs: The provider is solely liable for customer passwords and data classification.
The customer must guard the provider's physical data-centre doors.
Neither party handles security once a contract is signed.
why: Physical hosts and the hypervisor are the provider's job; identities, data, and guest settings stay with the customer, varying by service model.
example: On IaaS the provider patches the hypervisor, while the customer patches the guest OS and locks the storage bucket.
scenario: A provider secures the physical hosts, but a public storage bucket full of student data is traced to the customer's settings. Which model explains that split?
scenarioWhy: Platform security and customer configuration are split by the shared responsibility model.

definition: Hosting several customers on the same physical resources while keeping their workloads logically isolated.
wrongs: Giving each customer a private building and private power feed.
Running only one virtual machine on an entire data centre.
Printing a separate invoice without sharing any hardware.
why: Sharing hardware cuts cost, so isolation must stop one tenant from seeing another's data.
example: Two companies' virtual machines sit on one host but cannot read each other's memory.
scenario: Unrelated customers share one physical server, yet neither can read the other's disks. Which arrangement is that?
scenarioWhy: Shared hardware with logical isolation is multi-tenancy.

definition: Metering resource use so customers can be billed and can monitor what they consume.
wrongs: A flat fee with no record of CPU hours or storage.
A limit on who may call an API.
Replication of data into a second zone.
why: Cloud systems measure quantities such as hours, requests, and gigabytes.
example: A monthly bill lists 140 virtual-machine hours and 2 TB of object storage traffic.
scenario: The portal graphs gigabytes stored and CPU hours, and the invoice matches those figures. Which NIST characteristic is that?
scenarioWhy: Metering consumption for billing and monitoring is measured service.

definition: Letting a user provision computing resources without a human conversation with the provider.
wrongs: Waiting for a salesperson to rack a server next week.
Automatic growth of instances after a CPU alarm.
Reading monitoring graphs of resources that already exist.
why: A portal or API fulfils the request immediately, which is one of the NIST cloud characteristics.
example: A teaching assistant launches a database from a web console at midnight with no support ticket.
scenario: A student creates a virtual machine from an API at night without emailing the provider. Which characteristic is that?
scenarioWhy: Provisioning without human provider contact is on-demand self-service.

definition: Dynamically assigning capacity from a provider's shared pool, without a customer owning a specific physical server.
wrongs: Welding one application to one named physical machine forever.
Metering hours after the resources are already assigned.
Caching copies of files near end users.
why: The provider decides which physical resources serve a tenant and can reassign them as load changes.
example: A restarted virtual machine may land on a different host while keeping the same virtual disk.
scenario: Customers draw CPU from a common pool and are not promised one particular physical server. Which characteristic is that?
scenarioWhy: Dynamic assignment from a shared pool is resource pooling.

definition: Making cloud capabilities reachable over the network from standard client devices.
wrongs: Requiring a custom terminal that works only inside one machine room.
Shipping portable disks instead of using a network.
Limiting administration to a serial cable on the server.
why: Users reach the service with ordinary laptops, phones, or APIs across the network.
example: The same admin console works from a laptop at home and a phone on campus Wi-Fi.
scenario: Administrators manage the service from laptops and phones over the internet, not from a local serial console. Which characteristic is that?
scenarioWhy: Access from common networked clients is broad network access.

definition: A logically isolated virtual network, with the customer's own addresses and routes, inside a public cloud.
wrongs: The public internet with no customer-defined subnets.
A physical cage rented in a colocation hall.
A single security group rule on one network interface.
why: The customer chooses private address ranges, subnets, and route tables that other tenants do not share.
example: A course environment uses 10.1.0.0/16, with a public subnet for web servers and a private subnet for databases.
scenario: A class is given its own address plan and route tables inside a public provider, isolated from other accounts. Which network construct is that?
scenarioWhy: An isolated customer network inside a public cloud is a virtual private cloud.

definition: A policy that automatically adds or removes instances when a metric or schedule crosses a threshold.
wrongs: A human adding a server after reading an email alert.
Resizing one machine's memory by shutting it down for a manual change.
Moving traffic to a second region by editing DNS by hand.
why: The control loop watches signals such as CPU or request count and changes the instance count itself.
example: When average CPU stays above 70 percent for five minutes, the group launches two more web instances.
scenario: A group launches two more web instances after CPU stays high, then removes them when CPU falls. Which mechanism is that?
scenarioWhy: A policy that changes instance count from metrics is autoscaling.

definition: A set of geographically distributed caches that serve copies of content from a location near the user.
wrongs: The single origin database that holds the only copy of each row.
A load balancer inside one availability zone.
A batch job that transcodes video in the origin region.
why: Edge caches shorten the path for static or cacheable responses and protect the origin from repeated fetches.
example: A lecture video is fetched from a Singapore edge cache instead of the origin bucket in Ireland.
scenario: Students in many countries receive the same course video from a nearby cache rather than the origin bucket. Which service is that?
scenarioWhy: Nearby caches of content form a content delivery network.

definition: Keeping earlier copies of an object so an overwrite or delete can be undone.
wrongs: A point-in-time copy of a block volume attached to a virtual machine.
Replication of the current object to another region without history.
Compressing an object so it occupies less space.
why: Each write can create a new version under the same key, and an old version remains readable.
example: After a script overwrites notes.txt, the previous text is still available as an older version.
scenario: A bad upload replaces a key, but yesterday's bytes are still stored and can be restored. Which object feature allowed that?
scenarioWrongs: Cross-region replication of the latest copy
scenarioWhy: Retaining prior copies of an object is versioning.

definition: A point-in-time copy of a block volume that can be used to create a new disk later.
wrongs: Historical copies of a key-addressed object.
A live replica that always matches the current volume byte for byte.
A backup of only the virtual machine's metadata name.
why: The snapshot captures the volume's blocks at one moment, often stored durably apart from the attached disk.
example: Before a risky upgrade, an administrator snapshots the database volume and later restores a test disk from it.
scenario: Before patching, an operator saves a point-in-time copy of a virtual machine's disk and restores a test volume from it. Which copy is that?
scenarioWhy: A point-in-time copy of a block volume is a snapshot.

definition: Controls that decide which identities may perform which actions on which cloud resources.
wrongs: A network path that only checks IP packets for malware.
A bill that lists hours and gigabytes.
A status page showing region health.
why: Policies bind principals such as users and roles to permissions on services and data.
example: A teaching role may read one storage bucket but cannot delete the production database.
scenario: A policy lets a lab role read one bucket and denies it permission to terminate production instances. Which control plane is that?
scenarioWhy: Policies that bind identities to resource actions are identity and access management.

definition: A contract stating a measurable service target, such as monthly uptime, and the remedy if it is missed.
wrongs: An internal coding style guide with no provider commitment.
A monitoring graph that has no contractual target.
A discount coupon for unused credits.
why: The agreement makes availability or performance a commitment, often with service credits if the target is missed.
example: A provider promises 99.99 percent monthly uptime for a database and offers credit if uptime is lower.
scenario: A contract promises 99.9 percent monthly availability and credits the bill if the service falls short. Which document is that?
scenarioWhy: A contractual uptime or performance target is a service level agreement.

definition: Difficulty leaving a provider because a workload depends on that provider's proprietary services.
wrongs: Using only open formats that run unchanged on any cloud.
Keeping a tested exit plan and portable containers.
Paying month to month with no technical dependency.
why: Proprietary APIs, data formats, or managed engines raise the cost and time of a move.
example: An app built only on one provider's proprietary database API would need a rewrite to run elsewhere.
scenario: Moving a system would require rewriting calls that exist only at the current provider. Which risk is that?
scenarioWrongs: Month-to-month billing with no technical tie
scenarioWhy: Dependence on proprietary services that blocks a move is vendor lock-in.

definition: Moving an existing application to the cloud with little or no change to its architecture.
wrongs: Rebuilding the system as event-driven functions and managed services.
Retiring the application instead of hosting it.
Only backing it up without ever running it in the cloud.
why: Rehosting places the same application on cloud virtual machines to finish the move quickly.
example: A campus timetable server is copied onto a virtual machine and keeps its original monolith design.
scenario: A monolith is copied onto cloud virtual machines and keeps its original structure. Which migration style is that?
scenarioWhy: Rehosting an unchanged architecture is lift and shift.

definition: Sending overflow workload from a private cloud to a public cloud when local capacity is exhausted.
wrongs: Permanently moving every system to the public cloud.
Deleting overflow requests when the private cloud is full.
Caching static files at an edge node.
why: The private estate handles the base load, and the public cloud absorbs short peaks.
example: A university cluster sends extra rendering jobs to a public provider during thesis deadline week.
scenario: A private cluster is full, so extra rendering jobs run at a public provider until the peak ends. Which pattern is that?
scenarioWhy: Overflow from private capacity into a public cloud is cloud bursting.

definition: A discounted virtual-machine rate bought by committing to a term, often one or three years.
wrongs: Spare capacity that the provider may reclaim at any moment.
A function billed only for milliseconds of execution.
A free tier that ends after a small monthly quota.
why: The customer trades flexibility for a lower price on steady, long-running capacity.
example: A database that runs all year is covered by a three-year reservation at a lower hourly rate.
scenario: An always-on database receives a lower rate after the team commits to three years of capacity. Which purchase is that?
scenarioWhy: A long-term capacity commitment at a discount is a reserved instance.

definition: Spare cloud capacity sold cheaply that the provider can reclaim with little notice.
wrongs: A three-year discounted commitment the provider will not interrupt.
A dedicated host reserved for one customer only.
A serverless function that scales to zero.
why: The low price reflects the risk that the workload must stop or move when capacity is needed elsewhere.
example: A fault-tolerant render farm uses cheap reclaimable machines and restarts any interrupted frame.
scenario: A batch farm uses very cheap machines that the provider interrupts when it needs the capacity back. Which purchasing option is that?
scenarioWhy: Cheap spare capacity that can be reclaimed is a spot instance.

definition: Processing data close to where it is produced, instead of sending every event to a central region.
wrongs: Serving only cached copies of static files with no local computation.
Running all analytics in one central region.
Storing backups offline on tape.
why: Local processing cuts latency and the volume of data that must cross the wide-area network.
example: A campus gateway filters sensor readings and forwards only alerts, not every raw sample.
scenario: A factory gateway analyses sensor data on site and uploads only alerts, not every reading. Which approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Computation near the data source is edge computing.

definition: A managed front door that authenticates, throttles, and routes application API calls to backend services.
wrongs: A database engine that stores the application's tables.
A block volume attached to one virtual machine.
A batch scheduler for nightly jobs.
why: Clients call one endpoint, and the gateway checks identity, limits rate, and forwards the request.
example: Mobile apps call one HTTPS hostname that verifies tokens and routes each path to a different service.
scenario: All mobile clients call one hostname that checks tokens, limits request rate, and forwards each path. Which component is that?
scenarioWhy: A managed API front door for auth, limits, and routing is an API gateway.

definition: A buffer that holds work items so producers and consumers can run independently.
wrongs: A synchronous call that fails immediately if the receiver is down.
A shared file system used as the only database.
A load balancer session cookie.
why: The queue absorbs bursts and lets the consumer process messages at its own pace.
example: Web servers enqueue thumbnail jobs, and workers drain the queue even if a web server restarts.
scenario: Web uploads enqueue jobs that workers process later, so a slow worker does not fail the upload request. Which component sits between them?
scenarioWhy: A buffer that decouples producers from consumers is a message queue.

definition: A tenant whose heavy use of shared hardware degrades performance for other tenants on that host.
wrongs: A dedicated host with only one customer's virtual machines.
A region-wide outage caused by a fibre cut.
A billing error that overcharges a quiet account.
why: Contended CPU, disk, or network on multi-tenant hardware lets one workload steal performance.
example: One virtual machine's disk storm slows another customer's database on the same physical host.
scenario: One tenant's disk storm slows another tenant's database on the same physical host. Which problem is that?
scenarioWhy: One tenant hurting others on shared hardware is a noisy neighbour.

definition: Defining cloud resources in versioned text templates that a tool can create and update.
wrongs: Clicking each resource into existence and remembering the steps.
Writing only the application source code, not the environment.
Photographing the console as documentation.
why: Templates can be reviewed, repeated, and rolled back like application source.
example: A repository describes the network, virtual machines, and buckets, and a pipeline applies that description.
scenario: A pull request changes a text template, and a pipeline updates the network and servers to match. Which practice is that?
scenarioWhy: Versioned templates that build the environment are infrastructure as code.

definition: Running two production environments and switching traffic from the old one to the new one.
wrongs: Replacing binaries on the only live servers in place.
Sending every user a different experimental feature at random.
Keeping a spare region only for disaster recovery drills.
why: The idle environment is upgraded and tested, then the load balancer moves traffic across in one cut.
example: Version 5 runs in green while users still use blue; after checks, the balancer sends everyone to green.
scenario: The new release is fully installed in an idle environment, then the load balancer moves all users to it. Which release method is that?
scenarioWhy: Switching traffic between two live environments is blue-green deployment.

definition: A probe a load balancer or orchestrator uses to decide whether an instance should receive work.
wrongs: A yearly penetration test of the whole company.
A bill-review meeting with finance.
A checksum of a container image in a registry.
why: If the probe fails, the instance is marked unhealthy and new requests are sent elsewhere.
example: A balancer requests /health every 10 seconds and stops using any instance that returns an error.
scenario: A balancer calls /health every 10 seconds and removes an instance that keeps failing. Which mechanism is that?
scenarioWhy: A liveness probe that gates traffic is a health check.

definition: A requirement that specified data remain stored and processed in a chosen country or region.
wrongs: Replicating data to every region for the lowest latency.
The right of a user to download a copy of personal data.
Shredding disks when a lease ends.
why: Law or policy can forbid storing certain records outside a jurisdiction.
example: A university policy requires student records to stay in data centres inside the country.
scenario: Policy forbids storing admission records outside the country's provider regions. Which requirement is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping data inside a required geography is data residency.
